1: "Before I formed you in the womb I knew you." Jeremiah protests that he is too young. God touches his mouth and appoints him over nations, to pluck up and to plant.
God calls before we are ready, and promises, "I am with you."
2: God remembers Israel's early love like a bride's. Now they have forsaken him, the fountain of living water, and dug leaking cisterns for themselves.
Sin swaps the real source of life for things that cannot hold water.
3: Israel and Judah have behaved like unfaithful wives. Still God calls, "Return, and I will not be angry for ever. I will give you shepherds after my own heart."
God's appeal is that of wounded love.
4: "Break up your fallow ground; circumcise your hearts." An invader is coming like a lion. Jeremiah writhes in anguish.
The prophet feels the pain he announces.
5: Search Jerusalem's streets for one who does justice. The people have eyes and do not see; prophets lie, and "my people love to have it so".
A society can prefer comforting lies.
6: Jerusalem will be besieged. The leaders say "Peace, peace" when there is no peace. "Ask for the ancient paths, where the good way is, and walk in it."
Rest for the soul lies in the old, tested way.
7: At the Temple gate Jeremiah warns: do not chant "the temple of the Lord" while stealing, murdering and worshipping idols. You have made this house a den of robbers.
Jesus quotes this. Sacred places do not protect unrepentant people.
8: Even storks know their seasons, but the people do not know God's ways. "The harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved."
Jeremiah's heart breaks for his people.
9: "O that my head were a spring of water," to weep day and night. Let the wise not boast in wisdom, might or riches, but in knowing the Lord.
What matters is knowing God, who loves kindness and justice.
10: Idols are carved, decorated and nailed down; they cannot speak or walk. The Lord is the true and living God.
"It is not in man to direct his own steps."
11: Judah has broken the covenant and will face its curses. Jeremiah's own townsmen plot to kill him.
The prophet is like a gentle lamb led to slaughter.
12: Jeremiah complains to God. God answers: if running with men tires you, how will you compete with horses?
Honest questions are allowed. Harder trials are coming.
13: Jeremiah hides a linen cloth by the river and finds it rotten. So God will ruin Judah's pride. "Can the leopard change his spots?"
Israel was meant to cling to God as closely as a garment.
14: In a terrible drought the people plead. God says the prophets promising peace are lying in his name.
Not everyone who claims to speak for God does.
15: Jeremiah regrets being born to a life of conflict. "Your words were found, and I ate them, and they became my joy." God promises to make him a wall of bronze.
God's word sustains the lonely prophet.
16: Jeremiah is forbidden to marry or attend funerals and feasts, as a sign of what is coming. Yet God will one day bring Israel back.
The prophet's whole life becomes the message.
17: Cursed is the one who trusts in man; blessed the one who trusts in the Lord, like a tree by water. The heart is deceitful above all things. Keep the Sabbath.
Only God fully knows the human heart.
18: Jeremiah watches a potter rework a spoiled pot. Israel is clay in God's hand: he can change his plan if a nation repents.
It is not too late while the clay is soft.
19: Jeremiah smashes a clay jar before the elders: so will God break this city.
Once hardened, the pot cannot be remade.
20: The priest Pashhur beats Jeremiah and puts him in the stocks. Jeremiah cries, "You deceived me, Lord." Yet if he tries to keep silent, the word is like fire shut up in his bones.
21: King Zedekiah asks whether God will rescue them. Jeremiah answers that the city will fall; those who surrender will live.
An unwelcome truth is still the truth.
22: Jeremiah addresses Judah's kings: do justice. He condemns Jehoiakim for building a palace with unpaid labour.
"Your father did justice; is not this to know me?"
23: Woe to shepherds who scatter the flock. God will raise up for David a righteous Branch, called "The Lord is our righteousness". False prophets speak visions of their own minds.
24: Good figs stand for the exiles, whom God will bring back and give a heart to know him. Rotten figs stand for those left with Zedekiah.
The exile is, surprisingly, where hope lies.
25: Because Judah has not listened for twenty-three years, it will serve Babylon seventy years. All nations must drink the cup of God's wrath.
Judgement has a limit set by God.
26: After the Temple sermon priests and prophets demand his death. Officials recall the prophet Micah and spare him.
Speaking God's word can put your life at risk.
27: Jeremiah wears a wooden yoke and tells the kings to submit to Babylon.
Accepting God's discipline is the way to survive it.
28: The prophet Hananiah breaks the yoke and promises freedom within two years. Jeremiah says he has made the people trust a lie.
The pleasant prophecy was the false one.
29: Build houses, plant gardens, and pray for the city where you live. After seventy years God will bring you back. "I know the plans I have for you: plans for welfare, to give you a future and a hope."
God's good plans include a long wait.
30: A time of distress is coming for Jacob, but he will be saved from it. "I will restore health to you and heal your wounds."
God wounds in order to heal.
31: "I have loved you with an everlasting love." Rachel weeps for her children. God will make a new covenant, write his law on hearts, and remember sins no more.
Jesus names this covenant at the Last Supper.
32: With the city under siege and himself in prison, Jeremiah buys a field at God's command.
An act of hope: fields will again be bought in this land.
33: "Call to me and I will answer you." The city will again hear the voices of joy, and David will never lack an heir.
God's covenant is as fixed as day and night.
34: During the siege the people free their Hebrew slaves, then force them back when danger eases.
Repentance that lasts only as long as the emergency.
35: A clan keeps its ancestor's command never to drink wine. Judah will not keep God's.
36: Baruch writes Jeremiah's words and reads them out. King Jehoiakim cuts the scroll up column by column and burns it. Jeremiah dictates it again.
37: Accused of deserting, Jeremiah is beaten and jailed. Zedekiah asks him secretly, "Is there any word from the Lord?"
The king wants a word from God and lacks the courage to obey it.
38: Officials lower Jeremiah into a muddy cistern to die. Ebed-melech, an Ethiopian court official, pulls him out with ropes.
A foreigner shows the courage Judah's leaders lack.
39: The Babylonians break in. Zedekiah is captured and blinded. Jeremiah is freed.
Everything Jeremiah said has come true.
40: Jeremiah chooses to stay with the poor left in the land under the governor Gedaliah.
41: Ishmael assassinates the governor and many others.
42: The survivors ask Jeremiah to pray for guidance and promise to obey. The answer is to stay in the land.
They ask for God's will with their minds made up.
43: The leaders call Jeremiah a liar and take everyone to Egypt, including him.
Asking God and then ignoring the answer.
44: In Egypt the people insist on offering to a pagan goddess, claiming things went better when they did.
The exile has taught them nothing.
45: Jeremiah's weary secretary is told, "Do you seek great things for yourself? Seek them not." His life will be spared.
46: Egypt is defeated by Babylon at Carchemish and will be invaded.
Israel is told not to fear.
47: Waters rise from the north to overwhelm the Philistine cities.
God's sword does not rest until its work is done.
48: Moab, long at ease like undisturbed wine, will be poured out for its pride.
Even here God promises to restore Moab in the end.
49: Oracles on Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Kedar and Elam.
50: The hammer of the whole earth will be broken. Israel and Judah will come home weeping, seeking the Lord.
The instrument of judgement is judged in turn.
51: Babylon will sink and never rise. Jeremiah has the scroll tied to a stone and thrown into the Euphrates.
"Flee from Babylon; let each save his life."
52: A historical appendix: the siege, the burning of the Temple, the deportations, and the later release of King Jehoiachin.
The record proves the prophet right and closes with a small hope.
